meta.title: Notification System
meta.summary: One service that sends push and email for every team, respecting preferences, deduplicating retries and surviving provider outages.

functional: Internal services send push and email notifications through one API
Respect user preferences, opt-outs and quiet hours
Large marketing campaigns to millions of users
nonFunctional: Critical messages (one-time codes) arrive within ~5 s
No duplicate notifications when producers retry

scale.label: Campaign bursts
scale.value: Several million enqueued in minutes; ~60k/s at peak (5x)

slos.name: Critical delivery speed
slos.sli: Critical notifications accepted by the provider within the threshold of the API accepting them, divided by all critical notifications, measured by the workers from the accept time in the message

slos.name: Delivery rate
slos.sli: Notifications accepted by the provider divided by those attempted, measured at the workers, excluding invalid devices and addresses

slos.name: No duplicates
slos.sli: Notifications sent at most once, divided by all sent. Detective: the workers count repeats their sent markers catch, and a daily audit of provider send logs by message id counts any that slipped through.

slos.name: API accepts requests
slos.sli: POST /notify and /campaigns requests answered with a 2xx or a 4xx caused by the caller, divided by all, measured at the internal load balancer

alerts.when: Critical notifications later than 5 s burning the latency budget 14.4 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Login codes and security alerts are late, and the person is waiting.

alerts.when: Critical notifications later than 5 s burning the latency budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow drift, often workers under-scaled for the critical queue.

alerts.when: Oldest critical message above 30 seconds for 5 minutes
alerts.why: The cause behind late codes: workers are not keeping up with the critical queue.

alerts.when: Provider rejections burning the delivery budget 14.4 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Notifications are not reaching phones or inboxes.

alerts.when: Provider rejections burning the delivery budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A gradual loss of deliverability, such as a bad template or growing bounces.

alerts.when: API errors burning the error budget 14.4 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Producers cannot hand off notifications, so login codes are not even queued.

alerts.when: Push provider 5xx or timeout ratio above 10% for 5 minutes
alerts.why: The cause behind a delivery rate drop: APNs or FCM is failing, so messages wait in the queues.
A campaign is draining far slower than its quota allows (a 5M campaign takes under 20 minutes at 5k/s). Not urgent, but worth knowing.
Every message here failed all its retries and needs a human or a fix.

alerts.when: Email provider throttling above 5% for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Workers should pace themselves to the quota instead of hitting it.
If keys are evicted early, duplicates get through.

alerts.when: APNs certificate, FCM service account key or email sending identity expiring within 14 days
alerts.why: An expired credential silently stops a whole channel.

signals.name: Age of the oldest message
signals.why: The most direct measure of whether urgent messages are on time.

signals.name: Depth and arrival rate
signals.why: It should be empty. A steady trickle means a real bug.

signals.name: Unregistered rate (APNs 410, FCM 404)
signals.why: A rise means many users uninstalled or tokens have gone stale.

signals.name: Provider 429 share
signals.why: Shows whether pacing matches the provider quota.

signals.name: Repeats caught
signals.why: How often producers retry (API stage) and queues redeliver (worker stage); evictions here would let repeats through.

signals.name: Notifications by channel and priority
signals.why: Business view: which teams and campaigns drive volume, and whether critical traffic is a stable ~1%.

steps: Check the critical queue age: is it backing up?
Check provider latency and error codes.
Check that critical messages are not stuck behind preference or quiet-hours logic.

debug.symptom: A user got the same notification twice
steps: Find both sends by user and template in the worker logs; compare their message ids.
Different message ids: the producer retried without an idempotency key, or with a new one each time.
Same message id: the sent marker was missing; check dedupe store evictions and failovers at that time.
Check the bulk queue age and the email workers' send rate against the 5k/s quota.
Check provider 429s: the fleet may be pacing to a quota lower than it thinks.
Check that critical traffic is not unusually high, since it takes its share of the quota first.

nodes.label: Internal Services
nodes.description: Auth, orders, marketing and any other team that needs to notify users

nodes.label: Internal Load Balancer
nodes.description: Private L7 entry for producers; health-checks the API instances

nodes.label: Notification API
nodes.description: Validates, deduplicates, applies preferences, renders templates; ~60 instances at a 60k/s peak

nodes.label: Dedupe Store
nodes.description: Idempotency keys (API) and sent markers (workers), 24 h TTL

nodes.label: Preferences & Devices
nodes.description: Channels, opt-outs, quiet hours, device tokens

nodes.label: Critical Queue
nodes.description: One-time codes and security alerts, any channel; messages expire

nodes.label: Bulk Queue
nodes.description: Campaigns and other non-urgent messages, any channel

nodes.label: Push Workers
nodes.description: Long-lived services holding HTTP/2 connections to APNs and FCM; a dedicated pool for the critical queue so bulk pushes never delay it; leave the VPC through NAT

nodes.label: Email Workers
nodes.description: Drain the critical queue first; bulk sends paced to the provider's 5k/s quota

flows.title: Critical push (login code)
flows.summary: Deduplicate, check preferences, then a dedicated high-priority queue so nothing waits behind marketing.

steps.label: POST /notify
steps.detail: The auth service asks for a login code to be sent; the idempotency key makes its retries safe.

steps.label: to a healthy instance
steps.detail: Producers reach the API fleet through an internal load balancer that only sends to instances passing health checks.

steps.label: SET NX idem:… processing EX 60
steps.detail: Producers retry on timeouts. The first call takes a short claim; a repeat while it is held, or after it is marked queued, is acknowledged but not sent again. If this instance dies before queueing, the claim expires in 60 s and the producer's retry goes through, so a crash cannot swallow a login code.

steps.label: push on, 2 devices
steps.detail: Quiet hours apply to most messages, but security codes bypass them.

steps.label: enqueue
steps.detail: Critical and bulk traffic use separate queues, and a dedicated pool of workers drains the critical queue, so a 5M-user campaign cannot delay a login code. The message carries an expiry: a code nobody can use any more is dropped, not sent late.

steps.label: SET idem:… queued EX 86400
steps.detail: Only now is the key marked done, for 24 hours, which covers any producer's retry window.

steps.label: message n_8f31
steps.detail: Delivery from the queue is at least once.

steps.label: SET NX sent:n_8f31 sending EX 60
steps.detail: The worker-side check: a redelivered message finds the marker and is not sent twice. The short TTL means a worker that dies mid-send does not block the retry for long; after the provider accepts, the marker becomes sent for 24 h.

steps.label: send to 2 devices
steps.detail: Over persistent HTTP/2 connections to APNs and FCM, leaving the VPC through the NAT gateways.

steps.label: 200 / 410 Unregistered
steps.detail: APNs answers 410 when the token is no longer valid, for example because the app was uninstalled (FCM answers 404 UNREGISTERED).

steps.label: remove token apns:9f…
steps.detail: The stale device token is removed so it is not retried forever.

steps.label: "Tu código es 482913"
steps.detail: Apple delivers the push to the phone; the 200 above only meant APNs accepted it.

flows.title: Marketing email campaign
flows.summary: Filter by opt-in, spread sends under the provider's quota, retry with backoff, and park permanent failures in a dead-letter queue.

steps.label: POST /campaigns
steps.detail: Marketing schedules a campaign for a segment.

steps.label: filter opted-in (paged)
steps.detail: Pages through the segment, applying opt-outs, quiet hours by time zone and per-user frequency caps.

steps.label: 1.4M eligible
steps.detail: Users who opted out of marketing are dropped here, which is also a legal requirement in many regions.

steps.label: enqueue 1.4M (batches)
steps.detail: Each recipient becomes one message with its own id, sent in batches of 10. The queue absorbs the burst; nothing else has to scale for it.

steps.label: SET NX sent:… ×500 (pipelined)
steps.detail: The same worker-side check as for push: messages already sent are skipped.

steps.label: token bucket, 5k/s fleet-wide
steps.detail: Workers pace sends to the provider's quota instead of hammering it and getting throttled: the account's sending rate quota (assumed here to have been raised to 5k/s; SES accounts start at 1 message per second in the sandbox and need an increase request, also for the daily quota) is split across the worker fleet, and critical emails are taken first, so a campaign uses only what is left. 1.4M emails take about 5 minutes.

steps.label: 429 throttled (some)
steps.detail: Temporary failures are retried; permanent ones (invalid address) are not.

steps.label: retry with backoff + jitter
steps.detail: Delays grow 1 s, 4 s, 16 s … with randomness so retries do not arrive in a synchronized wave.

steps.label: after 5 attempts → DLQ
steps.detail: Nothing is silently dropped. An alert fires, and messages are replayed from the DLQ once the cause is fixed.

notes.text: Separate queues per priority isolate campaigns from critical traffic: both worker pools drain the critical queue first and keep part of each provider quota for it. Per-channel workers isolate providers: an email provider outage backs up email only, while push keeps flowing.

Delivery is at least once end to end. Idempotency keys at the API and sent markers per message id at the workers turn that into effectively once for users. The dedupe store is replicated asynchronously, so a failover can lose recent markers and let a rare duplicate through; that is what the 99.99% target allows.

Usual remedy for a long provider outage (not drawn): keep a second provider configured and switch over when the primary's error rate crosses a threshold. Until then, messages wait on the queues (kept for days), and critical ones are dropped once they expire.
Also enforce per-user frequency caps (for example, at most 3 marketing pushes a day) so many teams cannot collectively spam a user.

Not drawn here: an event log of every message's state (queued, sent, delivered, opened) from worker records and provider callbacks, for debugging and campaign analytics. Without it, delivery is only visible as provider acceptance.

There are no public callers: producers reach the API through an internal load balancer in the app subnet, with IAM or mTLS identifying each producing team. The only public subnet holds the NAT gateways the workers use to reach APNs, FCM and the email provider; the queues and preference store are reached through VPC endpoints.

questions.q: Why separate critical and bulk queues?
questions.a: A marketing campaign can enqueue millions of messages; in one shared queue a login code would wait behind them. A separate critical queue that every worker drains first, with part of each provider quota kept for it, keeps critical notifications fast regardless of bulk volume, and bulk can be throttled to protect providers and users.

questions.q: A service retries and sends the same notification request twice. How do you avoid notifying the user twice?
questions.a: Producers send an idempotency key; the API claims it in the dedupe store with a short expiry, marks it done for 24 h once the message is queued, and drops repeats. Workers also check a sent marker per message id before sending, because queues deliver at least once. The expiry is long enough to cover retries but short enough to keep the store small.

questions.q: APNs or FCM is down or rate limiting. What happens to the queued messages?
questions.a: Workers retry with exponential backoff and jitter; messages stay on the queue meanwhile. After a few failed attempts they go to the dead-letter queue for inspection and replay. Expired messages, such as a login code that is no longer valid, should be dropped rather than delivered late.

questions.q: How do you respect user preferences like quiet hours and opt-outs?
questions.a: Check preferences and channel opt-ins before enqueuing, and hold or drop non-critical messages during quiet hours in the user's time zone. Some messages, like security alerts, bypass marketing opt-outs but never the device or legal opt-outs. Unsubscribes must take effect quickly.

questions.q: How do you send a 10 million email campaign without getting blocked by providers?
questions.a: Throttle the bulk workers to the provider's allowed rate, spread the campaign over time, and warm up sending reputation gradually. Handle bounces and complaints by suppressing those addresses. The queue absorbs the backlog; nothing else needs to scale for it.

questions.q: How do you know notifications are actually being delivered?
questions.a: Record each message's state (accepted, sent, delivered, opened) using worker results and provider callbacks, in an event log this design does not draw. Alert on drops in delivery rate and on queue age for the critical queue, which is the symptom users feel. Per-provider dashboards show which channel is failing.
